query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high‐entropy alloys designed for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion is governed by the formation and maintenance of an adaptive, dual‐layer surface film. In this mechanism, a thin, continuous, and chemically enriched oxide (or hydroxide) layer rapidly forms (or reforms) at sites where wear disrupts the surface, thereby conferring corrosion resistance. Simultaneously, an outer mechanically compliant layer—whose microstructure is enriched in the most corrosion‐resistant elements (for example, Cr or Mo if present in the HEA)—provides local wear resistance. The constant removal and regrowth of this dual layer lead to a synergistic reduction in overall degradation compared to a material that lacks this dynamic film‐forming capacity.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy with a near-homogeneous equiaxed microstructure (e.g., a CrMnFeCoNi-based composition or similar) that contains a distribution of elements capable of forming stable, protective oxides under ambient conditions.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to controlled tribocorrosion testing where mechanical wear (e.g., via pin-on-disc or reciprocating sliding) is applied simultaneously with exposure to a corrosive electrolyte (e.g., 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution) under constant potential or free corrosion conditions.
generation.conditions: Ambient temperature (~25°C) and neutral pH; electrolyte containing chloride ions to simulate an aggressive environment; applied mechanical load and sliding speed chosen to generate measurable wear without immediately pulverizing the surface, so that film formation kinetics can be evaluated during cyclic damage and repassivation.
generation.structural_mediator: A dual-layer surface film consisting of an inner, adherent, passivating oxide (or hydroxide) enriched in the alloy’s most corrosion-resistant elements, and an outer strain-adaptive layer that temporarily forms and is continuously reformed upon mechanical disruption.
generation.mechanism: The alloy’s intrinsic chemical complexity promotes the segregation of elements that preferentially form protective oxides when the underlying material is exposed by wear. During sliding, mechanical abrasion intermittently removes the surface film. However, the alloy’s composition and stable microstructural state favor rapid re-oxidation, thereby re-establishing the protective barrier. This dynamic equilibrium between film removal (due to wear) and film reformation (via corrosion/passivation) yields a synergistic effect where the combined degradation rate (wear plus corrosion) is lower than the simple sum of their individual rates.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a matched baseline material (e.g., a conventional stainless steel or a HEA engineered without pronounced passivating element enrichment), the high-entropy alloy will exhibit a marked reduction in total material loss under identical tribocorrosion testing. Specifically, both the wear scar depth and the corrosion current density (or passive current) will be significantly lower in the HEA. Moreover, the degradation observed under simultaneous wear and corrosion conditions will be less than the additive effects of separate wear-only and corrosion-only tests.
generation.baseline: A control alloy that is compositionally similar but lacks the pronounced chemical complexity for dynamic dual-layer film formation (for example, a conventional stainless steel or a less optimized HEA without targeted corrosion‐resistant element enrichment), tested under the same tribocorrosion conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis should hold under environments where oxygen is available to support oxide formation and where the electrolyte is moderately aggressive (e.g., neutral chloride solutions). It may fail in conditions that either excessively accelerate wear (such as extremely high loads or speeds) or in environments (such as extremely acidic or alkaline media) that disrupt film formation or lead to uncontrollable film dissolution.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the specific film composition, the kinetics of film reformation under cyclic wear, and the precise contribution of microstructural heterogeneities (e.g., grain boundaries or minor secondary phases) to the overall resistance. The relative importance of the dual-layer film in mitigating tribocorrosion versus other potential factors (such as bulk alloy ductility or sub-surface work hardening) also remains to be fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a set of tribocorrosion tests in a well-controlled cell where both wear and corrosion are imposed simultaneously. Use surface analysis techniques (such as X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) or Auger electron spectroscopy) to characterize the continuously regenerating oxide layer and in situ electrochemical measurements (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization) to monitor corrosion behavior. Compare these results to tests where only wear or only corrosion is applied. A matched baseline alloy lacking the adaptive element segregation will be tested in parallel.
measurements: Mass loss measurements (gravimetric analysis) and wear scar depth profiling (via profilometry or microscopy)
Electrochemical measurements such as corrosion current density and open circuit potential during wear
Surface film characterization using XPS/Auger to detect chemical composition and thickness of the passivation layer
Friction coefficient and contact resistance measurements to assess wear performance
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimental data show that the HEA does not exhibit a lower combined degradation rate (i.e., wear plus corrosion) than what would be expected from the additive effects of wear-only and corrosion-only tests—or if no persistent, adaptive dual-layer film is identified on the worn surface—then the hypothesis is rejected.
